title: Orcas Use Fish as Bait to Catch Seagulls
sources: Science News, 17 Aug 2005, Susan Milius, 'Getting gull-baiting trick spreads among killer whales': MarineLand, Niagara Falls, Canada, captive orcas; Michael Noonan, Canisius College, watching the park's orcas for their calls; a young male baited gulls first, his younger half brother joined, then two adult females; Noonan calls it cultural transmission; biologist Galef finds cultural spread plausible but not confirmed by experiments; reported at the Animal Behavior Society meeting, not a peer reviewed paper

LiveScience via NBC News, 3 Feb 2006, Bjorn Carey, 'How killer whales trap gullible gulls': Marineland, Ontario, Canada, captive whales; whale spits fish on the surface, sinks and waits, lunges at the gull with open jaws, repeated again and again; the younger brother copied after a few months; the mother adopted it; soon all the orcas at the facility did it

Mongabay, 7 Sep 2005, 'Whale uses fish as bait to catch seagulls then shares strategy with fellow orcas': Noonan noticed it by accident while studying orca acoustics at Marineland, Niagara Falls, Ontario (captive orcas); young whale releases regurgitated fish, sinks, surges up when a hungry gull lands on the water; half brother copied within a few months; five whales now do it; Noonan: a tradition forming and spreading the way cultures do in humans

New Scientist via EurekAlert, 2006, Betsy Mason, killer whales and cultural learning: some researchers argue that many purported cases of cultural transmission can be explained by individuals discovering the skill on their own; Janet Mann (Georgetown) says for gull-baiting it would be hard to argue it is individual learning; Andrew Whiten (St Andrews) calls the observations particularly clear. Together with Science News (Galef: plausible, not confirmed by experiments) this supports 'some scientists are not sure whether the whales copied each other or each worked it out alone'
